lead: An aircraft makes alternating current (AC) and direct current (DC) power, but each load needs one exact form. A converter changes AC to DC, DC to AC, or AC to a lower AC voltage. A transformer rectifier unit (TRU) turns 115 V, 400 Hz AC into 28 V DC. An inverter turns DC back into 115 V, 400 Hz AC for standby instruments. An auto-transformer taps one winding to make 26 V AC for lighting and synchro reference. Some syllabi cover this chapter only briefly.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for where the AC and DC buses come from.

blocks.text: An inverter changes direct current (DC) into alternating current (AC). A static inverter uses an SCR (silicon-controlled rectifier) or transistor bridge to switch the DC input into a stepped AC waveform, then a filter smooths it. Output is 115 V root mean square (rms), 400 Hz (hertz), single-phase or three-phase, for AC instruments, synchros (small AC angle sensors) and the AC standby bus. Frequency comes from the switching control, not from a shaft. On generator loss the battery can drive the inverter through the DC bus; see 3.4.
Older rotary inverters used a DC motor driving an AC generator. Static inverters are lighter, need no brushes and start faster.

A TRU changes 115 V line-to-neutral, 400 Hz AC into 28 V DC. It has a three-phase transformer and a full-wave diode bridge. Ratings are often 100 A to 200 A. The output feeds the DC bus and charges the battery; see 3.3. The losses, Pac − Pdc, appear as heat.
Aircraft AC voltage is quoted line-to-neutral. A 115 V system has V<sub>LL</sub> = 115 × √3 = 199.2 V, about 200 V. Use V<sub>LL</sub> = 200 V in the formula below.
P<sub>dc</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub> × I<sub>dc</sub>; P<sub>ac</sub> = P<sub>dc</sub> / η; I<sub>line</sub> = P<sub>ac</sub> / (√3 × V<sub>LL</sub> × cos φ)
blocks.where: P<sub>dc</sub> is DC output power in W; V<sub>dc</sub> is DC voltage in V; I<sub>dc</sub> is DC current in A; P<sub>ac</sub> is AC input power in W; η is efficiency as a decimal; I<sub>line</sub> is line current in A; V<sub>LL</sub> is line-to-line AC voltage in V; for a 115 V aircraft AC system, V<sub>LL</sub> = 115 × √3 ≈ 200 V; cos φ is power factor.

blocks.text: An auto-transformer is one winding with a tap. It steps 115 V AC down to 26 V AC for instrument lighting and synchro reference. The voltage ratio is V<sub>2</sub> / V<sub>1</sub> = N<sub>2</sub> / N<sub>1</sub>, where V is voltage and N is turns. Part of the load current flows straight through the common section, so the winding carries only the difference of the two currents there and the unit is smaller and lighter than a two-winding transformer of the same rating. The price is no isolation: input and output share the winding, so a fault can pass across. Do not use it where isolation is required.

A current transformer (CT) senses load current. The cable carrying the load is the primary; the secondary gives a smaller current in a fixed ratio, for example 100 A to 5 A. A burden resistor turns secondary current into a voltage for indication or protection. The burden is the connected resistance; too large a burden distorts the signal. Never leave the secondary open while current flows, because a high voltage can appear.

examples.question: A transformer rectifier unit is rated 200 A at 28 V DC and is 92 % efficient. It is fed from a 200 V line-to-line (115 V line-to-neutral) three-phase AC bus at unity power factor. Find the DC output power, the AC input power and the line current drawn.
steps: DC output power: P<sub>dc</sub> = 28 V × 200 A = 5600 W.
AC input power: P<sub>ac</sub> = P<sub>dc</sub> / η = 5600 / 0.92 = 6086.96 W, about 6090 W.
Line current: I<sub>line</sub> = P<sub>ac</sub> / (√3 × 200 × 1) = 6086.96 / 346.41 = 17.57 A, about 17.6 A.
examples.answer: The TRU delivers 5600 W, draws about 6090 W from the AC bus, and takes about 17.6 A per line.

examples.question: An auto-transformer steps the 115 V AC bus down to 26 V AC for a panel-lighting load of 2 A. Ignoring losses, find (a) the turns ratio, (b) the load power, (c) the current drawn from the 115 V bus and (d) the current in the common section of the winding.
steps: (a) Turns ratio N<sub>2</sub> / N<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub> / V<sub>1</sub> = 26 ÷ 115 = 0.226.
(b) Load power = 26 V × 2 A = 52 W (VA, taking the lamps as resistive).
(c) Input power equals output power, so I<sub>1</sub> = 52 ÷ 115 = 0.452 A.
(d) The common section carries the load current minus the input current: 2 − 0.452 = 1.548 A, flowing against the input current in that section.
examples.answer: Ratio 0.226, 52 W, 0.452 A from the bus and 1.548 A in the common section. A two-winding transformer would carry the full 2 A in its own secondary and 0.452 A in a separate primary, which is why the auto-transformer is lighter.

traps: Treating an auto-transformer as an isolation transformer. It shares one winding, so a fault on the 115 V side can reach the 26 V side.
Using DC output power as AC input power, or dropping efficiency, when finding TRU line current.
Assuming inverter frequency follows battery voltage; the bridge control sets 400 Hz.
Leaving a CT secondary open, or choosing too large a burden.
Mixing 26 V AC instrument lighting with the 28 V DC bus.

quiz.q: What conversion does a TRU make?
quiz.a: 115 V, 400 Hz AC to 28 V DC.

quiz.q: What is the usual output of an aircraft static inverter?
quiz.a: 115 V rms, 400 Hz AC, single-phase or three-phase.

quiz.q: Why is an auto-transformer not an isolation transformer?
quiz.a: It uses one tapped winding, so input and output share a common circuit; a fault can pass across.

quiz.q: A TRU is rated 150 A at 28 V DC and is 90 % efficient. It runs from a 200 V line-to-line (115 V line-to-neutral) three-phase bus at unity power factor. Find its AC input power and line current.
Why must a CT secondary not be open while primary current flows?
quiz.a: The CT tries to force its ratio current; an open circuit gives a very high voltage, risking insulation failure and shock.

quiz.q: Why can a battery-fed inverter keep essential AC instruments alive after generator loss?
quiz.a: The inverter runs from the 28 V DC bus; the battery holds that bus up long enough for the standby source, so 115 V 400 Hz stays available.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern aircraft move toward variable-frequency AC and higher-voltage DC, so converters use silicon carbide or gallium nitride switches to cut weight and heat. More-electric aircraft replace hydraulic and pneumatic loads with electrical ones, raising converter ratings. Search for static inverter, active rectifier, TRU efficiency, current transformer burden and more-electric aircraft architecture.

figure.caption: Left: the TRU of Worked example 1 turns 6087 W from the 115/200 V AC bus (17.6 A per line) into 200 A at 28 V; the battery sits on the DC bus, and the inverter remakes 115 V 400 Hz for the standby bus from it. Right: Worked example 2's auto-transformer: 0.452 A in at 115 V, 2 A out at 26 V, and only the 1.548 A difference in the common turns.

spec.aria: Left: an AC bus feeds a 92 per cent TRU drawing 17.6 amps per line and delivering 200 amps to a 28 volt DC bus. A battery connects to the DC bus, which feeds an inverter and a 115 volt 400 hertz standby AC bus. Right: one coil tapped at 26 volts from a 115 volt supply, with 0.452 amps in, 2 amps out and 1.548 amps in the common section.
